title: About Tuberculosis

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium (or germ) called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In the United States, the majority of TB disease cases in people are caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Other mycobacteria (such as Mycobacterium bovis) can also cause TB disease in people.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: TB usually affects the lungs. TB can also affect other parts of the body, such as the brain, the kidneys, or the spine. TB can also affect multiple parts of the body at the same time. For example, TB can affect both the lungs and lymph nodes.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Not everyone infected with TB germs becomes sick. As a result, two TB-related conditions exist: inactive TB (or latent TB infection) and active TB disease.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: If not treated properly, TB disease can be fatal.

sections.heading: Inactive TB
sections.text: TB germs can live in the body without making you sick. This is called inactive TB, or latent TB infection. People with inactive TB are infected with TB germs, but they do not have active TB disease. They do not feel sick, do not have any symptoms, and cannot spread TB to others.

sections.heading: Inactive TB
sections.text: Without treatment, people with inactive TB can develop active TB disease at any time and become sick.

sections.heading: Active TB Disease
sections.text: TB germs become active if the immune system can’t stop them from growing. When TB germs are active (multiplying in your body), this is called active TB disease. People with active TB disease feel sick. They may also be able to spread the germs to people they spend time with every day. Without treatment, active TB disease can be fatal.

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: A cough that lasts three weeks or longer

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Chest pain

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Coughing up blood or sputum (phlegm from deep inside the lungs)

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Weakness or fatigue

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Weight loss

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Loss of appetite

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Chills

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Fever

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: Night sweats

sections.heading: Symptoms of active TB disease include:
sections.text: People with inactive TB do not have symptoms. However, without treatment, they can develop active TB disease and become sick.

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Anyone can get TB, but you might have a higher risk for TB if you:

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Were born in or frequently travel to countries where TB is common, including some countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Live or used to live in large group settings where TB is more common, such as homeless shelters, prisons, or jails

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Recently spent time with someone who has active TB disease

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Have a weaker immune system because of certain medications or health conditions such as diabetes, cancer, and HIV

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Work in places where TB is more likely to spread, such as hospitals, homeless shelters, correctional facilities, and nursing homes

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: TB is spread through the air from one person to another. The TB germs are put into the air when a person with active TB disease of the lungs or throat coughs, speaks, or sings.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: These germs can stay in the air for several hours, depending on the environment. TB germs are more likely to spread in indoor areas or other places with poor air circulation (such as a closed vehicle) than in outdoor areas. People who breathe in the air become infected with TB.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: People with active TB disease are most likely to spread TB germs to people they spend time with every day.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: If you are diagnosed with inactive TB, there are treatments available that can help protect you from getting sick with active TB disease.

sections.heading: Quick facts
sections.text: TB disease is one of the world's leading infectious disease killers.

sections.heading: Quick facts
sections.text: CDC estimates up to 13 million people in the United States live with inactive TB.

sections.heading: Quick facts
sections.text: Without treatment, 1 in 10 people with inactive TB will get sick with active TB disease. TB disease can spread to others and be deadly.

sections.heading: Quick facts
sections.text: In 2023, there were 9,633 cases of TB disease reported in the United States.

sections.heading: Testing
sections.text: CDC recommends that people that are at increased risk should be tested for TB. There are two types of tests that can find TB infection:

sections.heading: TB blood test
sections.text: The TB blood test is also called an interferon-gamma release assay or IGRA. The TB blood test measures how your immune system reacts to the germs that cause TB.

sections.heading: TB blood test
sections.text: If you have ever received a vaccine for TB, your health care provider should recommend the TB blood test. Unlike the TB skin test, TB blood tests are not affected by the TB vaccine (BCG vaccine).

sections.heading: TB skin test
sections.text: For the TB skin test, a health care provider uses a small needle to put some testing material under the skin. You will need to return to your health care provider in two to three days to see if there is a reaction.

sections.heading: If your TB blood test or skin test result is positive
sections.text: You have TB germs in your body. Your health care provider will do other tests to determine if you have inactive TB or active TB disease.

sections.heading: If your TB blood test or skin test result is positive
sections.text: These tests may include a chest x-ray, and a test of the sputum (phlegm) you cough up.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: If you have inactive TB, treating it is the best way to protect you from getting sick with active TB disease.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: If you have active TB disease, you can be treated with medicine. You will need to take and finish all of your TB medicine as directed by your health care provider. This is to help you feel better and prevent other people from getting sick.

sections.heading: Vaccines
sections.text: Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) is a vaccine for TB disease. The vaccine is not generally used in the United States. It is given to infants and small children in countries where TB is common. It protects children from getting severe forms of active TB disease, such as TB meningitis.

sections.heading: Vaccines
sections.text: Tell your health care provider if you have received the TB vaccine, especially if you are getting tested for TB infection because it can cause a false positive TB skin test reaction. TB blood tests are the preferred tests for people who have received the BCG TB vaccine.
